chapter: Ensemble, harmony and the Ory band
title: Harmony parts, rough ensemble and arranged New Orleans music
summary: They discuss loose harmony choruses, George Lewis's band as an intermediate style, Doc Evans's quartet-like harmonies, and Oliver and Jelly Roll arrangements.

bands.name: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I like the part he plays when all the whores like to obey our rights. Yeah. That's a beautiful part, the way they have that worked out in the band.

One thing I think about it, even in the harmony choruses, New Orleans' guys- Rough. Always rough. And they exploit the natural phrasing of their instrument instead of them trying to be quite together. Right. It's not quite unison. And something about that, it's a very loose unison.

I don't know. Well, not unison. Yeah. The parts, the good ones, you know, this is what I'm trying to assume. Like George's band, see, they're used to playing the strict ensemble style with lone harmony parts and everything, and it's catch as catch can. Yeah. Which is a kind of an intermediate style between the early Bowlin style and the finished full-time professionalism of an Armstrong, an Ori, or an Oliver, you know. Mm-hmm. That's where these bands kind of fall in between. Like I say, they were the second-liners. It's a casual band. Yeah. They were kind of the second-liners at the time these other men were playing, because the other men were older, too.

And there's really a distinguishing part. Like, that's the criticism that I hear so many of us. So the guys that admire the Oliver band and Louie's Hot Fives and Sevens don't care for George Lewis, because, well, I said, those were their interpretation of the real Rollins guys, and when the other bands are lacking changes and stuff, they're criticizing tremendously. Of course, I'm always fighting that battle up there, too, but that's another story. But that's where the harmonies work in. And yet, you take a harmony like Doc Evans, when his band plays the harmonies, it sounds like a baroque quartet, you know. Mm-hmm. But yet Ori would do the same thing with the same voice in the instruments. They retain the vibrato, and their attack is along the jazz lines. Not exactly on the beat, see. And not quite together.

And when we play, I never like to get myself, even on the harmony parts, I like to change it around as much as possible. Even just the accents. You can still play together, but change the accents around, and it makes it sound interesting. But all those Oliver tunes had them worked out. I like working man blues. And they were like, oh, you know, you can hear. And the breaks and stuff. That was all harmony parts. And then the most classic part in that whole tune, Richard M. Jones wrote that tune. They had the horns, the cornet, and the trombone, two cornets, and the trombone. La, la. That was worked out perfectly harmonically. The trombone player played a third above the two horns coming down. And Riverside Blues the same way. So those are the guys that were the very so-called the cream of the crop of the New Orleans men. Guys that had evolved themselves full-time professionally and had a complete knowledge of music more so than, say, like Jim. And that's where that came in. But I think a young band would do well to absorb all these different styles from all the good New Orleans bands that have played. From Oliver to Jellie Roll. Now there's a guy that just goes to show you what the best New Orleans men could do with arrangements. And look at the wonderful music that came out. It's completely arranged. And that just goes to show you. And that is kind of a stopgap for the guys that say, oh you can't arrange anything New Orleans and make it sound like real New Orleans music. But they did and you can't say it's anything but New Orleans music. And for those same three reasons. Attack, the tone of the instruments, the hot sound, and the phrasing.
